speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) among private hire car drivers and food delivery riders, what are their (i) mean and median employment duration and (ii) numbers according to age group; (b) whether the Ministry tracks the number and percentage of these riders who have moved on to permanent employment in other industries and, if so, what are these numbers in each of the past five years; and (c) whether the Ministry can provide customised career transition programmes for these riders to help them successfully find alternative employment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: asked the Minister for Manpower given that many freelancers, such as food delivery riders and point-to-point (P2P) drivers, do not determine the fees of services, but leave it to their platform partners' discretion, what are some of the safeguards that will be considered to ensure that these companies comply with their obligations should CPF contributions be made mandatory.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are subject to management control and are not able to set their own fees or remuneration, unlike the typical freelancers that we know.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, compared to employees, they receive lower job protections.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To address this, the Advisory Committee on Platform Workers was convened in September last year to look into three key areas of concern, namely: enhancing housing and retirement adequacy, providing financial protection in the event of work injury and strengthening representation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Since it was convened, the Committee has actively engaged stakeholders through dialogues as well as a public consultation paper.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To date, we have reached out to more than 20,000 platform workers and received about 1,200 submissions from them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Housing was the most commonly cited reason for wanting CPF contributions, followed by retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is not surprising, as platform workers today only make CPF contributions to their MediSave Accounts for their healthcare needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the coming months, we will continue with our engagement efforts and encourage all stakeholders, including platform workers, to share their views.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Committee is also aware that other surveys on platform work were commissioned and published recently, some of which were commissioned by the platform companies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These surveys vary in methodology and some have much smaller numbers of respondents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some of these surveys also did not capture the management controls and challenges that the platform workers face.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They need to maintain long and disciplined hours at work and must certainly be physically fit.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is significant physical and mental stress imposed on these workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While the surveys differ in their emphasis and findings, the one consistent feedback they note is that platform workers do experience greater uncertainty and would appreciate some aspects of what employees enjoy, such as the benefit of CPF contributions and work injury compensation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about how mandatory CPF contributions for platform workers could be implemented.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Without prejudging the outcome of the Committee’s deliberations, if this is implemented, we will develop appropriate mechanisms to ensure compliance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, platform workers already make mandatory CPF contributions out of their own earnings, although at a lower level of contribution, compared to an employee.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Committee is mindful that if mandatory CPF contribution for platform workers is introduced, platform companies will also have to start making contributions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While this will increase their business costs, it is no worse off than any other company employing workers in a similar sector, such as in logistics and transport.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Besides, platform companies already contribute CPF for their management executives and administrative staff today, a point which many of these riders whom I engage with, make as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They ask the question – as the ones who are bringing in revenue for the companies, risking themselves on the roads – why are they not given some of these basic things that employees working for the companies in the office actually also enjoy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But at the same time, the Committee is also aware that some platform workers are concerned about the impact on their take-home earnings.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This somehow also suggests that platform workers are not as well-paid, as some recent surveys have tried to portray.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the profile and longer-term career prospects of platform workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2021, the majority of those who depended on platform work as their main job were older residents aged 50 and over, although delivery workers tended to be slightly younger, with the majority aged below 40.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is not surprising, as riders have to maintain a certain level of physical fitness and toil for many hours a day covering long distances in order to keep their earning levels high, as I had earlier described.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The majority, or around 80% of those whose main job is a platform worker, view it as their preferred job.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2021, 8% of those who depended on platform work as their main job switched to work primarily as an employee – a slight increase from the 5% to 6% in recent years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to support platform workers to actively plan their careers and strengthen their employability, while respecting the preference of many to continue in platform work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For those looking for employment opportunities, Workforce Singapore and NTUC’s Employment and Employability Institute offer career matching services, including career coaching, employability workshops and job fairs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Workfare Skills Support Scheme and SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package are also available to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Singaporeans have called for more to be done for this group of precarious workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are often the forgotten heroes during the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, even as we gradually ease into the endemic phase of our fight against COVID-19, let us not forget the needs of this group of precarious workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As it continues to consult widely and facilitate deeper discussions, we will take in the feedback from platform workers and platform companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Regarding the figure given of 8% who have transitioned to permanent employment, would the Senior Minister of State have any data of the demographic profile of those who moved out of platform work into permanent employment of some sort or other?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are they the older ones or are they the younger ones?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would the Government consider, going forward, engaging more proactive communications to these platform workers, make them aware of these challenges and to stimulate them to think more about their long-term career prospects in other industries?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is drone delivery, for example, that is displacing some of these jobs already in some cities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are the concerns of some of the workers themselves: the fear of autonomous vehicles replacing their jobs and also, for the riders at least, it being such a physically demanding career, there is a question of how they can sustain this over a long period of time and make it a lifelong career.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Also, the risk of being injured any day and once you cannot physically subject yourself to that kind of toil anymore, the income would be impacted.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the other hand, the workers do value the flexibility and autonomy, to some extent, that they have.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is also a job with low barriers to entry and allows them quick access to ready cash to tide over a period of need.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And the Committee would continue to consult and engage our stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In terms of encouraging the workers to then look at a career transition, this is something that we have already put in place – some measures and schemes to support them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ultimately, it is also helping them to raise their awareness of what would make a sustainable career and help them to acquire the skills that are necessary to transit into a sector that may be of interest to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Skills upgrading is still core to the whole endeavour.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I think this is a complex issue.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I do not think there is a one-size-fits-all strategy that will cater to all and appeal to all of them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: My sense is that it is a very disparate group: some could be younger; some could be older; some could be more educated; some, because of their physical conditions, realise they need to transit to something that is less physically demanding.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think it is a broad spectrum, the point being that we need many different things to meet the different needs of different groups of people.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is unlikely to be a one-size-fits-all solution, nor a fixed archetype.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We did say that this is a job with low barriers to entry and, unfortunately, I do not think the companies themselves track such data, such as what is the status of this person's jobs before, during or after they join platform work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because, it is just as simple as downloading an app, getting a simple sign-up and they can start to engage in this kind of work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think the challenge is in getting this data.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will try to do some surveys on this but I think it is very hard for us to get very, very accurate data on how many percentage of them are ex-offenders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Not all of them will also engage in this full-time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some of them are doing it as a supplement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I have said, the landscape is very diverse and the challenge is to get a true fix.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At one point in time, we may get a single snapshot on how many ex-offenders are working in platform work, but they could easily exit the next day.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And more may come on the day after.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is where, whatever intervention we design, we need to have that flexibility to cater to the evolving needs of this group of workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Upstream intervention, including the Yellow Ribbon project, would be very important to make sure that ex-offenders, before they are re-integrated into society, are already given some degree of skills-training to allow them to, from the outset, look for jobs that are able to sustain them for the longer term and have employers who are prepared to take them on as employees so that there is perhaps less impetus for them to enter platform work as the job of choice when they get out into the rest of society.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think it takes all stakeholders, including the Singapore Prison Service, including employers who are enlightened, to engage and work with ex-offenders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because at this moment, some of them are doing this only as a very small segment of their working life.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, they could be working on a very casual basis.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Thus, they may not, actually, make contributions to CPF, if they are not working in this job as a full-time platform worker.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At best, it is probably about half of them doing so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We hope to get clearer data when we engage with the drivers, riders as well as the platform companies.
